case_source: In the matter of an application for stay. And in the matter of an application under Section 115(1) of the Code of Civil Procedure, 1908 for setting aside the Jt. and decree date. 22.5.80 and 28.5.80 respectively passed by Dist. Judge, Patuakhali in T.A. No 112/79 reversing those of Munsif, Patuakhali it, T.S. No. 3/77 passed in 27.10.79 and 3.11.79 in respectively.
full_judgment:
This Rule is directed against the appellate decree in a suit for declaration of the plaintiff's title to 2.39 acres of land representing 8 annas share in the holding recorded in C. S. Khatian No. 27 corresponding to R. S. Khatian No. 65 and S. A. Khatian No. 178 of Mouza Uttar Shubidkhali, under P.S Mrijagonj. The learned Munsif, 3rd Court, Patuakhali decreed the suit. On appeal the learned District Judge, Patuakhali reversed the judgment and decree of the learned Munsif and dismissed the suit.

2. It is undisputed that 4.94 acres of land in 18 different plots recorded in C.S. Khatian No. 27 belonged to Dhalai and Arabdi in equal shares. The plaintiffs are the successive heirs of Arabdi. Defendant Nos. 1.6 are the successive heirs of Dhalai and defendant No. 7 is the heirs of one Mokim Mridha. The lands of the disputed holding with a diminished area of 4.78 acres have been recorded in both the R S. and S.A. Khatians in the names of defendants 1-6 who are heirs and successors of Montazuddin, son of Dhalai, as well as in the name of Mokim Mridha, predecessor-in-interest of defendant No. 7. The plaintiffs were unaware of the wrong recording until 1.12.76 when the defendants denied their interest on the basis of the wrong record. The plaintiffs claimed that they were in continuous possession of their 8 annas share in the suit properties by cultivating paddy and living on the homestead plot.

Only the defendant No. 2 contested the suit by filing a written statement and denying the plaintiffs title and possession in the suit lands; He contends that Arabdi's son and only ultimate heir Tomiruddin mortgaged his 8 annas interest in the lands of the disputed khatian to one Nimchand Roy who in Mortgage Execution Case No. 117/18 auction purchased Tomiruddin's interest on 6.9 18 and took khas possession thereof on 13.4.1919. Thereafter he sold the interest under a registered kabala dated 19.5.1919 in favour of Dhalai who possessed the same. After the death of Dhalai his heirs and successive heirs including the defendants possessed the same. Ainuddin, a deceased grandson of Arabdi took settlement of .42 acres of land of the disputed holding for 12 years on payment of Tk. 50 as salami and at an annual rental of 9/- executing a registered kol karsha kabuliyat on 18.9.29 in favour of Montaruddin, son of Dhalai. The Kabuliyat was executed by Ainuddin on his own behalf and on behalf of plaintiff Nos. 1 & 2, then minors. This under-tenancy fell into arrears of rent and in Rent Execution Case No. 273/44 Montazuddin auction purchased the land and took delivery of possession thereof on 19.6.44 by evicting the plaintiffs and since then the defendants are in possession of the lands of the entire holding.

3. The plaintiffs examined 4 P.Ws. and the contesting defendant examined 3 D.Ws and exhibited several documents in support of their respective cases. The learned Munsif on consideration of the oral evidence on record found that the plaintiffs were in possession of suit land. The learned District Judge, on the other hand, considered the exhibits filed by the contesting defendant showing that Nimchand Roy, the decree-holder auction purchased the 8 annas share of Tomiruddin, heir of Arabdi and also showing that he took delivery of possession through Court on 13.4.1919. He noticed the certified copy of the sale certificate. He also noticed the registered kabala dated 19.5.1919 executed by Nimchand Roy in favour of Dhalai in respect of his auction purchased 8 annas share. The karsha kabuliyat executed by Ainuddin was also noticed by the learned District Judge. He also noticed the certified copy of the writ of delivery of possession of .42 acres of land on 19.6.44 by evicting the plaintiff Nos. 1 & 2 and Ainuddin. The learned District Judge found that the registered kabala dated 19.5.1919 and the registered kol karsha kabuliyat came from proper custody and the other documents were certified copies of Court documents. He then discussed the evidence of P.Ws. and found that they were not competent to say anything about the transactions of mortgage and auction sale taking place as far back as in 1918 and 1919. The learned District Judge also found that except for homestead plot No. 1388 the plaintiff's evidence on possession was not convincing On the other hand, the contesting defendant's evidence on possession was satisfactorily proved by the D.Ws., except with regard to homestead plot No. 1388 which, even according to D.W. 2, was in possession of the plaintiffs. The learned District Judge held that since the defendants' possession in at least 8 annas share of the disputed khatian is undisputed, the plaintiffs have the burden to prove that they possess the remaining 8 annas share in suit They have failed to prove the same, except that they are in possession of homestead plot No. 1388. The learned District Judge was also of the view that the plaintiffs have failed to rebut the presumption that the R.S. and S.A. records were correct. He, however, held that the suit was not barred by limitation. The learned District Justice set aside lodgment and decree of the learned munsif with the modification that the plaintiffs right, title and interest in plot no. 1388 in suit was declared and the suit was decreed to that extent only. Thereafter the plaintiffs obtained the present Rule.

4. Mr. Khondkar Mahbubuddin Ahmed, learned Advocate for the petitioners submits that the court of appeal below committed an error of law apparent on the face of the record by approaching the suit from a wrong view of onus which has completely vitiated his findings. Mr. Ahmed submits that admittedly the C.S. Khatian record Arabdi, the predecessor-in-interest of the plaintiffs as 8 annas co-sharer of the disputed khatian. If it is the case of the defendants that a mortgage, a mortgage execution case, an auction sale, a sale of the auction purchased land, a kol karsha kabuliyat of a part of the purchased land and finally a rent execution case in respect of the kabuliyat lands took place subsequent to the C.S. operation, the onus was on the contesting defendant not only to prove these subsequent developments but also conclusively to prove that after each alleged event the defendants predecessor had obtained actual physical possession of the 8 annas share of Arabdi. Instead, the learned District Judge has proceeded from the wrong standpoint that since till defendants are in possession of their 8 annas share, which is undisputed, it is for the plaintiffs to prove that they possessed the remaining 8 annas share in suit. It is this wrong view of onus which has prompted the court of appeal below to merely weigh on balance the evidence of P.Ws. and D.Ws. on possession of the suit land except the homestead plot No. 1388. Had the learned District Judge approached the question from the right standpoint, namely, that it is for the contesting defendant to prove the transactions subsequent to C.S. operation as well as possession be would have looked into the evidence of actual physical possession of the predecessors of the defendants after each alleged event. He having not done so, Mr. Ahmed submits, the appeal should be re-heard by the appellate Court below keeping the question of onus uppermost in view.

5. It is true that the plaintiffs have based their claim on the simple proposition that they are the heirs and successors of the 8 annas recorded tenant in the C.S khatian The C.S. khatian supports their case. It is however the contesting defendant's case that several developments have taken place after the C.S. operation resulting in the transfer of ownership and possession of the 8 annas share of Arabdi in the hands of the defendants predecessor. To prove that point, the defendants have filed a number of documents, as already stated, which have been believed by the Court of appeal below. The presumption of correctness of entry in the C.S. Khatian was never in doubt. The defendants also admit the correctness of the entry in the C.S. Khatian. The defendant’s documents have convinced the Court of appeal below that subsequent to the C.S. operation the defendants' predecessor acquired ownership and possession of the 8 annas share of Arabdi. What the Court of appeal below held in substance is that the latter developments after the C.S. operation have been proved by the contesting defendant. Under the circumstances, it is difficult to hold that the defendant has not discharged his onus to prove the subsequent developments.

<u>6. As far as possession is concerned both sides have adduced evidence. When both sides adduce evidence the question of onus loses it importance and the court has to weigh the evidence on record and come to a decision on the basis of preponderance of evidence. Obviously the Court of appeal below was not impressed with the evidence of P.Ws. on the subject. His council that the plaintiffs were not in possession of the suit land except the homestead plot No 1388 is therefore based on an appreciation of evidence over which this Court sitting in the revisional jurisdiction will not interfere.</u>

7. Mr. Ahmed's next submission is that the Court of appeal below committed an error of law apparent on the face of the record by dismissing the plaintiffs suit against the defendant Nos. 1 and 3-7 who did not contest the suit. It is only the defendant No. 2 who contested the suit by filing a written statement. The defendant No. 2 did not contest the suit on behalf of the other defendants. He filed power only on his own behalf and the written statement was also signed only by him. The other defendants were, therefore, non-contesting defendants and since they did not contest the suit at all, the learned District Judge should have decreed the suit against them. Mr. Ahmed refers to Order 1, rule 12 of the Code of Civil Procedure which provides that where there are more defendants than one, any one or more of them may he authorised by any other of them to appear, plead or act for such other in any proceeding. If the defendant No. 2 was so authorised by the other defendant then his defence would have been the defence of the other defendants, and the other defendants would have stood or fallen along with the defendant No. 2 But in the present case. Mr. Ahmed submits the defendant No. 2 was not authorised in terms of Order 1, rule 12 of the Code of Civil Procedure. Mr. Ahmed next draws my attention to Order 15. rule 2 of the Code of Civil Procedure which provides that where there are more defendants than one, and any one of the defendants is not at issue with the plaintiff on any question of law or of fact, the Court may at once pronounce judgment for or against such defendant and the suit shall Proceed only against the other defendants. Mr. Ahmed argues that the expression "any one of the defendants" not at issue with the plaintiff" refers to the non-contesting defendants as well, because they are not at issue with plaintiff.

<u>8. The argument is attractive, but hardly commends to me In my view a defendant is "not at issue with the plaintiff" only if before or during framing of issues he comes and tells the Court either by filing a written statement or orally that he does not pick up any issue with the plaintiff Thus, in a money suit the defendant may come and tell the Court that he admits the claim of the plaintiff but only asks for installments. To make a defendant one who is ''not at issue with the plaintiff" he must appear and say so. A non-correcting defendant has several options up his sleeves. He can come up any moment to say that he did not receive the summons of the suit. He can come at the close of the trial to say that he received information about the suit only recently and he wants to contest the suit. At the first hearing of the suit which is the subject matter of Order 15, rule 2 of the Code of Civil Procedure it cannot be presumed against the non-contesting defendant that he was not at issue with the plaintiff.</u>

<u>9. Moreover, the plaintiff may file a suit against several defendants and none of them may appear. The plaintiff has still the burden to prove his own case in an ex parte proceeding. If he cannot prove his own case even in an ex parte proceeding the suit cannot be decreed against the non-contesting defendants.</u>

10. In the present case the plaintiffs have not been able to prove their case of tide and possession not only in so far as the contesting defendant No. 2 is concerned, but also in so far as the other non-contesting defendants are concerned. Can it be said then that the suit should be decreed against the non-contesting defendants, simply because they did not contest the suit? I am clearly of the opinion that the suit cannot be so decreed.

For all the above reasons I do not find any ground for interference in the Rule.

In the result the Rule is discharged without any order as to costs. The judgment and decree of the learned district Judge are affirmed.

Let the records be sent down immediately.

End.
